Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

Grok Build Uploaded Entire Git Repositories to xAI Storage, Not Just Files It Read

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 3 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

xAI's Grok Build coding CLI was uploading entire Git repositories, full commit history and all, to a Google Cloud Storage bucket run by xAI, not just the files a coding task needed. A researcher publishing as cereblab, testing version 0.2.93, captured one of those uploads, cloned the git bundle out of the intercepted request, and pulled back a file the agent had been told in plain terms not

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Grok Build CLI presence & execution (0.2.93/0.2.99) — exposed-endpoint discovery
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Grok Build CLI uploads full repo/git-bundle to xAI storage channel (grok-code-session-traces) · [LLM] Grok Build CLI local staging of session/codebase archive (metadata.json → gs://grok-code-session-traces)
Grok Build CLI uploads full repo/git-bundle to xAI storage channel (grok-code-session-traces) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the wire signal of Grok Build's wholesale codebase exfiltration: the grok CLI POSTing git bundles/tar archives to cli-chat-proxy.grok.com/v1/storage and PUTting chunks into the Google Cloud Storage bucket grok-code-session-traces. This is the channel that shipped 5.10 GiB of unread source (73x ~75MB chunks) in cereblab's 12 GB test, independent of the model turn on /v1/responses. Rationale: Anchored on the two uniquely-named article/gist IOCs — host cli-chat-proxy.grok.com and GCS bucket grok-code-session-traces on the /v1/storage channel — plus the grok process reaching storage.googleapis.com. These strings appear nowhere else in benign traffic, so any hit is the repo-upload behavior. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/cereblab/dc9a40bc26120f4540e4e09b75ffb547 • https://github.com/cereblab/grok-build-exfil-repro • https://cyberpress.org/grok-build-cli-repositories-env-secrets/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1567
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer intentionally using Grok Build after xAI re-enables the upload flag server-side (the 0.2.99 binary still contains the upload code)
  • Corporate proxy replaying/caching a prior grok session URL during a proxy config test
  • Security researcher reproducing cereblab's mitmproxy harness on a sanctioned canary repo
  • Network telemetry from a decommissioned test host that had grok installed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and DeviceName !in~ ("secresearch-lab01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the developer/host and confirm grok (~/.grok/bin/grok) is installed; pull the RequestURL/SentBytes to gauge how much source left the machine. 2) Contain: block cli-chat-proxy.grok.com and the grok-code-session-traces bucket at the proxy/egress; have the user run `/privacy` in the CLI to delete synced data and uninstall until policy is set. 3) Hunt: enumerate every credential in the affected repo AND its git history (committed-then-deleted secrets ride along) and rotate them; pivot on other hosts resolving cli-chat-proxy.grok.com to find all exposed repositories.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any ("cli-chat-proxy.grok.com", "grok-code-session-traces"))
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "grok" and RemoteUrl has "storage.googleapis.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("grok-code-session-traces", "cli-chat-proxy.grok.com")
    or DestinationHostName has_any ("grok-code-session-traces", "cli-chat-proxy.grok.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), TotalSentBytes=sum(tolong(SentBytes)), SampleUrl=any(RequestURL)

Grok Build CLI presence & execution (0.2.93/0.2.99) — exposed-endpoint discovery AIReconnaissance High
Enumerates hosts running the Grok Build coding CLI so the SOC can find every machine that may have shipped source to xAI and remediate (run /privacy, rotate creds). Anchors on the grok binary at ~/.grok/bin/grok and its platform-specific names; the upload code still ships in build 0.2.99, held off only by a server flag xAI can flip back. Rationale: Uses the exact install path (~/.grok/bin/grok) and platform binary names from cereblab's gist plus the named vulnerable versions (0.2.93, 0.2.99). It is an exposure-discovery hunt, not an attack alert — the value is enumerating every dev machine that must run /privacy and rotate secrets. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/cereblab/dc9a40bc26120f4540e4e09b75ffb547 • https://github.com/cereblab/grok-build-exfil-repro
ATT&CKT1119 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Developers who have already remediated (ran /privacy) but binary still present
  • Sanctioned enterprise deployment on zero-data-retention (ZDR) accounts where xAI states no code/trace is stored
  • CI runner images that pre-bake the grok CLI

| where FolderPath endswith "/.grok/bin/grok"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is the xAI binary via FolderPath (~/.grok/bin/grok) and capture the account/host and product version. 2) Contain: on non-ZDR accounts, direct the user to run `/privacy` to disable retention and delete synced data; block egress to cli-chat-proxy.grok.com until governance approves the tool. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against the UC1 network alert to confirm whether a repo actually uploaded, then scope credential rotation to the repos those developers had open.

Grok Build CLI local staging of session/codebase archive (metadata.json → gs://grok-code-session-traces) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the collection/staging step that precedes the upload: the grok CLI writing its session_state archive and a metadata.json whose per-file paths point at gs://grok-code-session-traces/ under the ~/.grok working directory. Catching the staged bundle on disk detects the behavior even when TLS-inspected egress is unavailable. Rationale: Uses the article/gist's named staging artifacts — metadata.json with gs://grok-code-session-traces/ paths and the session_state archive — scoped to writes by the grok process under ~/.grok. Medium confidence because metadata.json is a generic filename, so the grok-process anchor is what makes it article-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/cereblab/dc9a40bc26120f4540e4e09b75ffb547 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/grok-build-uploads-entire-git.html
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated application writing a generic metadata.json into a coincidental path (mitigated by the grok-process anchor)
  • Grok CLI legitimate operation on ZDR/enterprise accounts where no data is retained server-side
  • Backup/sync tooling snapshotting the ~/.grok directory
  • Developer manually inspecting a captured grok bundle from the cereblab repro harness
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "grok" and (FolderPath has "/.grok/" or FolderPath has "grok-code-session-traces")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the staged metadata.json / archive path and confirm it references gs://grok-code-session-traces/ and enumerates the developer's actual source files. 2) Contain: block egress to cli-chat-proxy.grok.com and storage.googleapis.com/grok-code-session-traces, run /privacy to delete synced data, and quarantine the staged archive. 3) Hunt: treat every file (and git-history secret) named in the metadata.json as exposed — rotate all credentials committed to that repo, including secrets deleted from the working tree but still in history, and check UC1 for a matching upload.

| where FileName =~ "metadata.json"

Exposure to revoked vulnerable UEFI shims (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed endpoints that Defender TVM flags as carrying the ESET-reported vulnerable UEFI shim bootloaders (versions <=0.9) covered by CVE-2026-8863 and CVE-2026-10797. These devices remain exploitable for Secure Boot bypass until Microsoft's June 9 2026 dbx revocation (KB5101650) is applied, so this is a posture hunt to prioritise dbx rollout. Rationale: Pivots on the two CVE IDs assigned by CERT/CC (VU#616257) and ESET to the reported shims; TVM CVE mapping is high-fidelity for prioritising which hosts still need the June 2026 dbx update. No FP concept — it is a vulnerability-inventory lookup. Cross-checked against: • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/11-old-microsoft-signed-linux-uefi.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/eset-uefi-secure-boot-bypass/
ATT&CKT1542 T1542.003
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM CVE-to-firmware mapping lag means recently-patched (dbx applied) hosts may still show as vulnerable for one scan cycle
  • Linux/dual-boot hosts legitimately shipping shim as part of the distro but already on shim >=15.7
  • Devices where the third-party UEFI CA is disabled in firmware are not actually exploitable but may still list the shim software
  • Air-gapped or offline devices whose TVM data is stale
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device trusts the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 third-party cert and whether the June 9 2026 dbx update (KB5101650) is installed. 2) Contain: schedule/push the dbx revocation update; where BitLocker is present, validate recovery keys are escrowed before the dbx change to avoid boot lockout. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, pivot to UC-2/UC-3 to check whether a rogue shim was actually written to the ESP or the partition was mounted, and review boot integrity / measured-boot logs.

Vulnerable UEFI shim/GRUB bootloader written to the EFI System Partition AIInstallation Medium
Detects a shim or GRUB2 EFI bootloader binary (shimx64.efi, grubx64.efi, mmx64.efi, bootx64.efi and 32-bit variants) being created or modified under an \EFI\ path — the 'bring your own vulnerable shim' technique ESET describes, where an attacker drops a Microsoft-signed but pre-revocation shim onto any UEFI system to bypass Secure Boot. Highest signal on Windows-only endpoints that should never have Linux shim/GRUB binaries on the ESP. Rationale: Uses the exact shim/GRUB EFI filenames from the shim ecosystem the article names (shim + second-stage GRUB2) constrained to the \EFI\ system-partition path. On a Windows-managed fleet, a Linux shim/GRUB binary appearing on the ESP is a strong 'attacker staged a pre-revocation shim' signal rather than any Microsoft boot component (bootmgfw.efi). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1542
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Linux install or dual-boot setup writing shim/GRUB to the ESP
  • OEM/firmware recovery or imaging tooling refreshing fallback \EFI\Boot\bootx64.efi
  • Endpoint backup/restore software that snapshots and rewrites the ESP
  • Legitimate shim upgrade (>=15.7) pushed by a Linux distro package manager on genuinely dual-boot hosts
  • Enterprise Linux deployment/MDT task sequences staging boot files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("grub-install","bootmgr.exe","setup.exe","dism.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcess writing the file — legitimate installers (setup.exe, grub-install, firmware updaters) vs. an interactive shell/LOLBin; compute and compare the file's Authenticode hash against the 11 dbx-revoked hashes from the ESET advisory. 2) Contain: if the writer is untrusted or the hash matches a revoked shim, isolate the host, preserve the ESP contents, and force the dbx (KB5101650) update to neutralise the shim. 3) Hunt: check UC-3 for a preceding mountvol /S on the same host, review boot configuration (bcdedit) changes, and look for known bootkit artefacts (Bootkitty, HybridPetya, BlackLotus).

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimia32.efi","grubx64.efi","grubia32.efi","mmx64.efi","mmia32.efi","bootx64.efi","bootia32.efi")
| where FolderPath has @"\EFI\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimia32.efi","grubx64.efi","grubia32.efi","mmx64.efi","mmia32.efi","bootx64.efi","bootia32.efi")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\EFI\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EFI System Partition mounted via mountvol /S (rogue shim staging) AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution of mountvol.exe with the /S switch, which mounts the normally-hidden EFI System Partition to a drive letter — the prerequisite step an attacker uses on Windows to drop a pre-revocation shim onto the ESP before deploying a bootkit. This LOLBin flag is extremely rare in normal operations, making it a high-signal hunting pivot. Rationale: mountvol /S is the documented, rarely-used command to expose the EFI System Partition on UEFI systems; pairing it with the shim-write in UC-2 reconstructs the on-host staging chain for ESET's bring-your-own-shim bypass. Command flag is concrete and article-adjacent (ESP manipulation), not a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting boot/BCD issues or manually inspecting the ESP
  • OEM firmware/BIOS update utilities that mount the ESP to stage capsule updates
  • Backup/imaging software mounting the ESP for full-disk capture
  • Windows servicing or driver-signing workflows that touch the ESP
  • IT scripts that mount the ESP to repair bootmgfw.efi after a failed update
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and user launching mountvol /S — a scripted/interactive shell (cmd, powershell, unknown binary) is far more suspicious than a signed OEM updater; note any drive letter assigned. 2) Contain: if launched outside an approved change window or by an untrusted parent, isolate the host and inspect the newly-mounted ESP for shim/GRUB binaries (feed into UC-2) before dismounting. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host and 10-minute window for .efi writes to \EFI\, bcdedit boot-order changes, and any of the 11 revoked shim hashes; verify dbx (KB5101650) status.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mountvol.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/s"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mountvol.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/s"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: EFI System Partition Mounted via mountvol /S
id: 4d7c9a11-6e02-4b3f-8f5a-2b0c7d1e9a34
description: Detects mountvol.exe using the /S switch to mount the EFI System Partition, a staging step for writing a pre-revocation UEFI shim to the ESP (ESET Secure Boot bypass, CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/
  - https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1542
  - attack.t1542.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\mountvol.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/S'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:*\\mountvol.exe OR @Image:*\\MountVol.exe OR @Image:*\\MOUNTVOL.EXE) (@CommandLine:*/S* OR @CommandLine:*/s*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\mountvol\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\s\/s\b/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="mountvol.exe" AND Processes.process="*/S*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="mountvol.exe" AND Processes.process="*/S*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8863", "CVE-2026-10797")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8863", "CVE-2026-10797")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-8863", "CVE-2026-10797")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-8863", "CVE-2026-10797")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["AE75F0D82BA3DF824FBFC69340CC3B4D66C598373B1AB54CDB6C8BFD83A6B961", "7B2A3F5C96F95BD8086CE54B0825E300F9C8F11FE3401BB631B3215C8DE9EB10", "EB86FA1386FE6E4533B8B938DCC1250616D2F1C14C15E2FCF80834A161018A0A", "FD23D6E57DE6F4E1F9D7118DA1C5F31A8AF6BE5E5D9E8170F9493447268D50C5", "A0DE9333442C1BF9349A460141AE5E80F911955C6506040FA3D021BF6C1AE3E4", "95B6D71FC0C0F8C5E1533A37AEF92CF6B0C961E2CC612A97117FA6759CE5FC06", "236A9CB0D71951C36398A32EB660CE2CD4A52CCFA7CF751CC6A35D9DE549E19B", "5E594C448760A3135B1A3A83E07A4F2E6FBE49414EF2C7CAB1CBA77F284FA63B", "8A964D5F8373948D20A1D4296FB92E545DAD4617A0C810F3B934B53D98AE8963", "410260B1B6F5AF5FBEEB9EA3220658435E876CB3247126EE907A437F312DB373", "96275DFD6282A522B011177EE049296952AC794832091F937FBBF92869028629"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Smart Install exploitation (CVE-2018-0171) — inbound TCP/4786 from untrusted source AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound TCP port 4786 (Cisco Smart Install / SMI) traffic reaching network infrastructure from external or untrusted source IPs, the entry vector FSB Center 16 (Static Tundra) uses to trigger config extraction and RCE on unpatched Cisco IOS/IOS-XE devices per the FBI advisory referenced in this article. Article-specific because it targets the exact CVE (CVE-2018-0171) and Smart Install protocol the FSB actors abuse, not generic scanning. Rationale: Uses CVE-2018-0171 and its fixed protocol port (Cisco Smart Install / TCP 4786) named in the FBI advisory the article cites; SMI has no legitimate internet-facing use, so external inbound 4786 is high-fidelity. Defender KQL left empty because the targets are Cisco routers/switches, not Defender-managed endpoints. Corroborated via FBI IC3 PSA and Cisco Talos Static Tundra reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2025/russian-government-cyber-actors-targeting-networking-devices-critical-infrastructure • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2018-0171 • https://research.splunk.com/stories/cisco_smart_install_remote_code_execution_cve-2018-0171/
ATT&CKT1190 T1602.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) probing 4786 from an internal scanning subnet
  • Cisco DNA Center / Prime Infrastructure legitimately using Smart Install from a management station
  • External security-research internet scanners (Shodan/Censys) hitting a perimeter device
  • Penetration-test engagement using smi_check / SIET tooling
  • Misconfigured management traffic traversing an untrusted transit link
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<add authorized scanner IPs>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/untrusted and identify the DestinationIP device model and IOS version; check if Smart Install is enabled (`show vstack config`) and whether the device is unpatched for CVE-2018-0171. 2) Contain: block TCP/4786 at the perimeter, disable Smart Install (`no vstack`) on the device, and rotate device credentials/SNMP strings. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'SNMP config exfiltration' and 'SNMP scanning' from the same SourceIP; review the device running-config for unauthorized ACL/local-account/TFTP changes and evidence of SYNful Knock implants.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 4786
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| summarize Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Targets=make_set(DestinationIP, 50) by SourceIP, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by Attempts desc

Network device configuration exfiltration via SNMP config-copy / TFTP-FTP egress (Static Tundra) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts network devices copying their running-config off-box to an external host over TFTP/FTP, or Cisco syslog referencing the attacker config filenames config.bkp/output.txt — the SNMP config-copy MIB exfiltration technique FSB Center 16 uses to collect device configurations en masse. Article-specific: mirrors the advisory's 'copy its configuration to a file and transfer it to an attacker-controlled VPS or compromised FTP server' behaviour. Rationale: Combines the advisory's exact exfil filenames (config.bkp / output.txt) and the SNMP config-copy-to-TFTP/FTP behaviour from CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB; a router/switch pushing running-config to a public IP over TFTP(69)/FTP(21) is rare and high-signal. Sigma omitted because the highest-fidelity form (Cisco syslog string match + external-egress correlation) is not a clean single-event standard logsource. Corroborated via MITRE T1602.002 and Cisco Talos Static Tundra reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1602/002/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://industrialcyber.co/threats-attacks/russian-fsb-center-16-exploits-decade-old-cisco-flaw-in-cyber-espionage-campaign-to-target-critical-infrastructure/
ATT&CKT1602.002 T1602.001 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled network backup jobs (SolarWinds NCM, RANCID, Oxidized) legitimately copying configs — but normally to an INTERNAL server
  • Admin manually running `copy running-config tftp:` to an authorized internal TFTP host
  • Firmware/IOS image staging over TFTP during a maintenance window
  • A misconfigured backup target pointing at a cloud/public IP
  • IPAM or monitoring tooling pulling configs via SNMP for inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("<approved-tftp-server-ip>", "oxidized", "rancid", "solarwinds"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source device and destination IP; confirm the destination is external and NOT an approved config-backup server, and check whether the copy used config.bkp/output.txt naming. 2) Contain: null-route/block the external destination, revoke SNMP write access and rotate all SNMP community strings, and isolate the device for forensic capture of running vs startup config. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC 'Cisco Smart Install exploitation' and 'SNMP scanning' from the same actor infrastructure; enumerate every device whose config left the org in the same window and check for unauthorized accounts/ACL/GRE-tunnel changes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("config.bkp", "output.txt")
    or (SyslogMessage has "running-config" and SyslogMessage has_any ("tftp", "ftp") and SyslogMessage has_any ("copy", "ccCopy"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SNMP sweep from external source using default community strings (FSB Center 16 recon) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single external source IP issuing SNMP (UDP/161) requests against many internal network devices — the proxy-fronted SNMP scanning FSB Center 16 uses to find poorly configured devices that accept common/default community strings before pulling their configs. Article-specific: models the advisory's 'scan for Internet IP ranges with active SNMP agents that accept common or default community strings' step. Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's SNMP v1/v2 default-community-string scanning: one external source touching >=25 distinct internal SNMP agents (UDP/161) is a scan, not management. Threshold-based aggregation so Sigma is intentionally skipped. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because SNMP scanning of network gear surfaces on firewall/flow telemetry, not endpoint EDR or AWS logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250820 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1602/001/ • https://media.defense.gov/2026/Jul/09/2003959498/-1/-1/0/CSA_IMPROVE_ROUTER_HYGIENE.PDF
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046 T1602.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized NMS/monitoring platform (SolarWinds, PRTG, LibreNMS, Zabbix) polling many devices over SNMP — normally from an internal poller, not external
  • Approved external managed-service provider (MSP) monitoring the estate over SNMP
  • Vulnerability scanner performing SNMP enumeration during a sanctioned assessment
  • Internet-wide research scanners (Shodan/Censys) touching perimeter interfaces
  • IPAM/asset-discovery tool running a scheduled SNMP inventory sweep
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<approved-external-MSP-poller-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate/enrich SourceIP (ASN, threat-intel, proxy/VPN reputation) and confirm it is not an approved internal or MSP poller; note how many and which device types were swept. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, migrate devices to SNMPv3 with authPriv, and remove default/common community strings (public/private). 3) Hunt: check whether any swept device subsequently exported its config (UC 'config exfiltration') or received inbound TCP/4786 (UC 'Smart Install'); treat any device that responded to a default community string as potentially enumerated and audit its running-config.

| order by AgentsScanned desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0171", "CVE-2008-4128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0171", "CVE-2008-4128")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

DeviceProcessEvents

148 npm Packages Disguised as Student Proxies Turned Browsers Into a DDoS Botnet

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A campaign of 148 npm packages disguised as student web proxies turned visitors' browsers into a distributed denial-of-service botnet for roughly two weeks in May, according to new research from&nbsp;JFrog. The packages did not go after the developers who might install them. The operators used the registry as free hosting for a booby-trapped proxy site and let the students who came to dodge

Browser/Node contact with Lucide student-proxy DDoS campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the Lucide (lucideproxy) campaign's clustered infrastructure — the Wisp flood endpoint lunaron[.]top, the still-live monetization/script hosts, and the G-Core Labs IP that fronted 90 of 93 deployment hostnames. Article-specific because these exact domains/IP are JFrog+SafeDep-confirmed campaign IOCs with no legitimate business use. Rationale: Pivots on the exact JFrog/SafeDep-confirmed campaign endpoints — Wisp flood host lunaron[.]top, monetization hosts woofbeginner[.]com and c.vipersfutbol[.]com the current build still reaches, commit-email domain geeked[.]wtf, and the G-Core IP 92.38.177[.]17 that resolved 90 of 93 deployment hostnames. None have legitimate enterprise use, so any contact is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://safedep.io/malicious-npm-terminal3airport-proxy-adware-spam/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-148-malicious-npm-packages-masquerading-as-student-proxies-turn-browsers-into-ddos-botnet

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or SOC analyst deliberately detonating the proxy in a sandbox that ships telemetry to the same tenant
  • Threat-intel or URL-scanning tooling (urlscan.io agent, VirusTotal retro-hunt box) resolving the domains for enrichment
  • A student personal device on guest WiFi loading the proxy site (expected true positive, but low security impact vs corporate asset)
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked lookup as an outbound event
  • Passive-DNS or newly-registered-domain feed pre-fetching the domain

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("urlscan.exe", "vt-cli.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (browser vs node vs script engine) and confirm the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP matches a campaign IOC, not a lookalike; check whether the connection succeeded or was blocked at proxy/firewall. 2) Contain: block all five IOCs (lunaron.top, woofbeginner.com, c.vipersfutbol.com, geeked.wtf, 92.38.177.17) at DNS/egress, and on the affected browser clear cache + local storage and unregister any service worker registered by a tutoring/proxy domain. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host for npm installs of the named packages (UC2) and for sustained connection floods to lunaron.top or cdn.caan.edu (UC3/UC4); check whether any build agent pulled the packages into a lockfile.

Install of named Lucide malicious student-proxy npm packages AIDelivery High
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm installs or node_modules writes of the specific packages JFrog flagged as still-malicious in the campaign — charlie-kirk, ilovefemboys, miguelphonk. Article-specific because these package names are named IOCs; charlie-kirk was still serving malicious versions 2.0.0 and 3.0.1 as of 2026-07-14. Rationale: Uses the three package names the article explicitly cites (charlie-kirk, ilovefemboys, miguelphonk), gated on package-manager execution context so it fires on the actual dependency pull, not incidental text. High fidelity because these are confirmed IOCs and charlie-kirk was verified still-malicious on 2026-07-14. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://safedep.io/malicious-npm-terminal3airport-proxy-adware-spam/

Browser HTTP flood against nursing-school domain cdn.caan.edu AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a compromised browser tab acting as a Lucide DDoS bot: the G2 loader's archived payload fired a fresh one-million-character no-cors POST at cdn.caan.edu every 500ms. Detects sustained high-count outbound connections to caan.edu from a browser process — a rate no human browsing produces. Rationale: Grounded in the archived May-30 G2 payload JFrog recovered: a no-cors POST of a one-million-character string to cdn.caan.edu every 500ms (~2 MB/s per tab). The count threshold captures the automated flood cadence while the browser-process gate excludes server-side traffic — a shape no legitimate user generates against a single nursing-school CDN. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-148-malicious-npm-packages-masquerading-as-student-proxies-turn-browsers-into-ddos-botnet
ATT&CKT1498.001 T1583.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate student/staff member of Chamberlain/CAAN nursing programs heavily using cdn.caan.edu courseware (verify request cadence and payload size)
  • A synthetic-monitoring or uptime probe pointed at caan.edu from a corporate browser-automation host
  • A load/performance test a partner org runs against caan.edu with authorization
  • Browser prefetch/prerender inflating connection counts on a single legitimate page visit
  • A shared NAT/proxy egress IP aggregating many users' normal traffic to caan.edu above the threshold (pivot on SourceHostName not SourceIP)
Suppression filter
| where SourceHostName !has "synthetic" and SourceHostName !has "loadtest"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser is the initiator and the connection rate/payload matches a flood (hundreds of POSTs, ~2 MB/s upload) rather than normal courseware use; identify what page/tab the user had open. 2) Contain: block cdn.caan.edu and the campaign domains at egress, kill the offending browser tab/process, and clear the browser's cache, local storage and any tutoring/proxy service worker. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the Wisp flood to lunaron.top (UC4) and for the npm package install (UC2); notify caan.edu's abuse contact if your egress contributed to their flood.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "caan.edu"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe")
| summarize connCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 5)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| where connCount > 100    // script POSTs every 500ms -> >100 conns within minutes; humans never sustain this to one edu host
| order by connCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has "caan.edu" or RequestURL has "caan.edu"
| summarize reqCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Methods = make_set(RequestMethod, 5)
    by SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName
| where reqCount > 100    // sustained flood; 500ms POST cadence far exceeds any human page load
| order by reqCount desc

Browser Wisp/WebSocket control-plane flood to Lucide endpoint lunaron.top AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the I2 module's control-plane attack: each infected browser opened up to 1,024 (config: 30) staggered WebSocket connections to a Wisp endpoint on lunaron.top and hammered it with CONNECT/CLOSE frames every 100ms. Detects an abnormal burst of concurrent connections from one browser to lunaron.top / the campaign IP — the socket-exhaustion signature. Rationale: Uses the JFrog-reconstructed I2 config values verbatim — a Wisp WebSocket target on lunaron[.]top with a per-browser socket count of 30 (cap 1,024) — and the G-Core IP 92.38.177[.]17. A browser opening 30+ concurrent sockets to one host and holding them is the socket-exhaustion control-plane signature, not human browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/148-npm-packages-disguised-as-student.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/150-npm-packages-promises-wi-fi-bypass-students/
ATT&CKT1498.001 T1499.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A browser with many tabs to a single legitimate high-concurrency web app (SPA with websockets, video conferencing) crossing 30 concurrent sockets — but not to lunaron.top
  • A shared NAT egress IP aggregating multiple browsers' connections (pivot on SourceHostName/DeviceName, not SourceIP)
  • A researcher detonating the proxy in a monitored VM
  • Connection-pooling proxies that multiplex and inflate observed connection counts to the campaign IP
  • The campaign IP later reassigned by G-Core to a benign tenant (re-validate the IP is still campaign-attributed before alerting)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-analysis"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the 30+ concurrent connections originate from one browser process to lunaron.top / 92.38.177.17 and are sustained (Wisp CONNECT/CLOSE every 100ms), not a one-off burst; identify the open tab. 2) Contain: block lunaron.top and 92.38.177.17 at egress, terminate the browser process/tab, and clear the browser cache, local storage and any tutoring/proxy service worker. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the parallel cdn.caan.edu HTTP flood (UC3), the initial npm package install (UC2), and sweep egress for other hosts hitting the campaign IP; report the abusive Wisp traffic if lunaron.top is a third-party victim.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "lunaron.top" or RemoteIP == "92.38.177.17"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe")
| summarize connCount = count(), DistinctPorts = dcount(LocalPort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| where connCount > 30    // archived Wisp config aimed each browser at 30 sockets (cap 1024)
| order by connCount desc
CommonSecurityLog

| summarize connCount = count(), DistinctSrcPorts = dcount(SourcePort), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName
| where connCount > 30    // Wisp config: 30 concurrent sockets per browser
| order by connCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Microsoft Maps Three Salesforce Attack Paths Tied to a Year of ShinyHunters Activity

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 10 use cases 4 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers whose methods line up with the data-extortion group&nbsp;ShinyHunters&nbsp;have spent the past year walking into corporate Salesforce environments without exploiting a single flaw in the platform. The way in has been the trust the organization had already extended, usually through the OAuth connections that tie Salesforce to the apps and third-party vendors around it. In&nbsp;

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Salesforce consent to spoofed 'Data Loader' connected app (UNC6040 vishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated Salesforce Aura/GraphQL guest scraping past 2,000-record limit · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Compromised vendor OAuth integration (Drift/Gainsight/Klue) mass Salesforce export · [LLM] Salesforce SOQL secret-hunting across Case/support objects (AWS/Snowflake/VPN) · [LLM] Anti-forensic deletion of Salesforce async query/bulk job records · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Salesforce consent to spoofed 'Data Loader' connected app (UNC6040 vishing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts OAuth consent grants inside Salesforce to a connected app branded as 'Data Loader' but not the legitimate Salesforce client, the payoff of the ShinyHunters/UNC6040 vishing calls. Surfaces the granting user, source IP and geo so an analyst can confirm the call/consent chain. Rationale: Keys on the article's explicit lure — a connected app 'dressed up as Salesforce's own Data Loader tool' — corroborated by GTIG/Mandiant which note the consented app's name/branding differs from the legit Data Loader. Consent event ties the malicious app to a specific user identity, IP and geo. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2025/250912.pdf • https://appomni.com/blog/detecting-unc6040-vishing-in-salesforce-oauth-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1078.004 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately installing/authorizing the genuine Salesforce Data Loader connected app for data migration
  • Data migration or ETL project onboarding a Data Loader-style integration
  • Sandbox refresh where connected apps are re-consented
  • Third-party MSP performing an authorized bulk data load
  • Renamed internal integration that happens to contain 'Data Loader' in its label
Suppression filter
| where not (ConsentedApp has "Data Loader" and IsAdminOperation == true and CountryCode in ("US","GB"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the consenting user and confirm out-of-band whether they authorized a Data Loader app in the last 24h; check if the client_id matches Salesforce's official Data Loader vs an arbitrary/attacker app id and whether a vishing call preceded it. 2) Contain: in Salesforce Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, revoke the app's tokens and block the app; force re-auth / reset the user's session. 3) Hunt: review that app's ApiEvent/BulkApi activity for enumeration and secret-hunting SOQL, and check for other users who consented to the same app id.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Consent","Connected","OAuth","Authorize","Grant")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend ConsentedApp = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ConnectedAppName), ObjectName)
| where ConsentedApp has "Data Loader"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ActionType, ConsentedApp, ObjectId
| order by Timestamp desc

CloudAppEvents

| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend ConsentedApp = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ConnectedAppName), ObjectName)
| where ConsentedApp has "Data Loader"
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ActionType, ConsentedApp, ObjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised vendor OAuth integration (Drift/Gainsight/Klue) mass Salesforce export AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts high-volume SOQL/Bulk-API data pulls performed by trusted vendor connected apps named Drift, Gainsight or Klue — the integrations whose stolen OAuth/refresh tokens ShinyHunters (UNC6395/Storm-3138) turned against downstream Salesforce orgs. Flags export volume far above a normal integration sync. Rationale: Names the exact compromised vendor apps from the article (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue) and thresholds on export volume — the Drift token theth alone reportedly exposed 700+ orgs by querying/exporting Salesforce objects, so bulk row counts by these apps are high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.illumio.com/blog/the-master-key-problem-what-the-salesloft-breach-reveals-about-an-ongoing-threat
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1530 T1567
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate scheduled Gainsight/Drift sync ingesting large object volumes after a new deployment
  • Initial full-history backfill when a vendor integration is first connected
  • Analytics/BI vendor app running a large nightly report export
  • Data migration event temporarily spiking a vendor app's query volume
  • Sandbox seeding where a vendor app bulk-reads production data
Suppression filter
| where not (AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue") and SrcIps has_any ("<known-vendor-egress-range>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the connected app and compare the query volume and source IP/ASN to its 30-day baseline; confirm whether the vendor has disclosed a token-theft incident (Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue advisories). 2) Contain: revoke the app's OAuth/refresh tokens in Salesforce Connected Apps OAuth Usage and disable the integration user; rotate any credentials the exported objects could contain. 3) Hunt: pivot to the SOQL bodies for secret-hunting patterns (AWS/Snowflake), and check for query-job deletions the actor uses to cover tracks.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","Bulk","Report","Export","Query")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend AppName = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ClientName))
| where AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue")
| extend Rows = toint(coalesce(Raw.RowsProcessed, Raw.NumberOfRecords, Raw.RowCount))
| summarize TotalRows = sum(Rows), Queries = count(), SrcIps = make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AppName, AccountDisplayName
| where TotalRows > 50000 or Queries > 500   // 50k rows / 500 calls = well above a normal chat/CI integration sync cadence
| order by TotalRows desc

Salesforce SOQL secret-hunting across Case/support objects (AWS/Snowflake/VPN) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SOQL/API queries whose body searches Salesforce records (support cases, notes) for embedded secrets — AWS access keys, Snowflake tokens, VPN and password strings — exactly the loot UNC6395 sifted for after stealing Drift tokens. Content match on the AKIA prefix and secret keywords. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit statement that operators ran SOQL to sift support cases for AWS keys, Snowflake tokens and passwords; the AWS 'AKIA' access-key prefix plus 'snowflakecomputing' are low-FP content anchors that ordinary CRM queries rarely contain. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.illumio.com/blog/the-master-key-problem-what-the-salesloft-breach-reveals-about-an-ongoing-threat
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1213 T1530
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running a legitimate secret-sprawl audit across Salesforce records
  • DLP or CASB vendor scanning case bodies for exposed credentials
  • Support agent legitimately searching a case containing the word 'password'
  • Integration that indexes case text for search and echoes keywords in query logs
  • Pentest/red-team engagement authorized to hunt for embedded secrets
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("dlp","casb","secaudit") or IsAdminOperation == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full SOQL body and the querying identity/app — confirm whether the actor is a vendor integration token (see Drift/Gainsight/Klue) or an interactive session, and whether results returned rows. 2) Contain: revoke the querying app/user tokens and immediately rotate any AWS keys, Snowflake tokens or VPN creds that were stored in the matched objects. 3) Hunt: enumerate all objects returned, check for downstream use of the harvested keys in AWS CloudTrail/Snowflake login history, and look for query-job deletion covering the activity.

Anti-forensic deletion of Salesforce async query/bulk job records AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts deletion/abort of Salesforce async query, Apex and Bulk-API job records — the track-covering step the Salesloft Drift operators used, deleting their query jobs to slow investigators. Keys on delete/abort actions targeting job objects rather than a bare column. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated anti-forensic behaviour ('deleting their query jobs to slow down anyone investigating'); scopes to async/bulk job object types so it fires on evidence removal, not routine record deletes. Fixes prior schema error by matching on ActionType values instead of a non-existent 'Delete' column. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion
ATT&CKT1070 T1070.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin housekeeping that clears completed/failed async Apex jobs
  • Bulk-API integration aborting a stuck or duplicate job
  • Scheduled cleanup script pruning old BackgroundOperation records
  • DevOps pipeline aborting bulk loads during a failed deployment
  • Salesforce support aborting a runaway job during a case
Suppression filter
| where not (IsAdminOperation == true and AccountDisplayName has_any ("integration","svc","automation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who deleted/aborted the job and whether the same identity ran large SOQL/Bulk exports just before the deletion (correlate on user/app + preceding 1h). 2) Contain: preserve remaining Real-Time Event Monitoring logs, revoke the identity's tokens, and enable log export/retention to prevent further tampering. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the deleted jobs' query scope from surviving ApiEvent/BulkApi telemetry and check for secret-hunting SOQL and vendor-token abuse by the same actor.
